column4: Mary’s mother says that when she “put her down” she was female; childbirth supplies another bodily use of the section’s وضع root, though this ayah does not itself call the pregnancy a load.

Elderly women may lay aside their outer garments without displaying adornment; garment and the named setting-down verb meet here, but unlike the section’s dictionary bundle the garment is neither filled nor carried.
After recounting Abraham’s argument, God says, “We raise in degrees whom We will”; the named root denotes conferred rank, helping distinguish the raised remembrance from physical lifting.
God raises some people above others in degrees in order to test them in what He gave; elevation is rank joined to responsibility, not release from accountability.
In Joseph’s story God says, “We raise in degrees whom We will”; the rise in standing follows divinely given wisdom and parallels remembrance elevated as honor.
God raises some people above others in degrees so they may employ one another; this social differentiation is another real sense of رفع and sets a boundary around the section’s personal honor.
Joseph raises his parents upon the throne; the physical act also enacts public honor, bridging literal lifting and the section’s metaphorical elevation of a name.
The honored pages of 80:13 are “raised and purified”; this ayah’s own contribution is elevation of the written Reminder itself, close to raised dhikr.
God tells Jesus, “I am raising you to Me”; the same divine act toward a prophet raises the person rather than the person’s remembrance, marking a concrete lexical boundary.
“God raised him to Himself” again applies رفع to Jesus’s person; it clarifies that prophetic elevation can mean removal of the person, whereas the section explicitly names dhikr as the lifted object.

The accusation that God’s hand is fettered is answered by saying the accusers’ hands are fettered while His hands are outspread; the polemic uses bodily restraint to distinguish constricted giving from divine generosity.
On that Day none binds as God binds; divine fastening supplies a general judgment counterpart to the section’s concrete shackle and cord image.
Believers are told to go forth “light and heavy”; duty continues across bodily and material conditions, setting carried difficulty beside the section’s divinely relieved mission.
Those who ask the Prophet for transport leave weeping when he has nothing on which to carry them; the ayah reverses the burden scene into people needing a bearer so they can join the task.
Within nursing and family support, no soul is charged beyond capacity and neither parent is to be harmed through the child; it applies the load boundary to an embodied care burden.
The commands concerning an orphan’s property and just measure are followed by “We charge no soul except to its capacity”; moral duty is measured rather than made crushing.
Those who believe and act rightly enter the Garden after the reminder that no soul is charged beyond capacity; attainable obligation stands against a back-breaking load.
God charges no soul beyond capacity, and a record with Him speaks truth; measured burden and exact accounting meet in the same ayah.
The Prophet is told to fight while being charged only for himself and to urge the believers; his mission includes leadership, but his accountable burden cannot be reassigned to the group.
“Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned”; personal deeds become bodily-seeming restraint, joining the section’s nontransferable moral load to its fetter image.

God joins believing descendants to their families without diminishing anyone’s deeds, then says each person is held in pledge for what he earned; gracious reunion does not transfer accountable burdens.

Immediately after 53:38’s rule that no bearer bears another’s burden, this ayah adds that a human has only what he strives for; it specifies the positive ownership corresponding to nontransferable liability.
The one whose sin encompasses him belongs to the Fire; guilt is pictured as surrounding the person rather than sitting on the back, another concrete relation between wrongdoing and body.
God and His angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to bless and greet him; the ayah enacts his elevated remembrance across divine, angelic, and human speech.
The Prophet is promised that his Lord may raise him to a praised station; bestowed elevation and public praise directly parallel a remembrance raised for him.
God promises the Prophet mighty help; this supplies direct divine support for the mission alongside 48:2’s forgiveness and the section’s removed strain.
God directly clears the Prophet of the accusation of madness by His grace; the defense restores the addressee’s public name, a specific aspect of elevated remembrance.
The promise of an unfailing reward follows the defense in 68:2; its own contribution is enduring divine recompense accompanying restored honor.
God declares the Prophet to possess tremendous character; this positive divine testimony supplies the honored reputation raised above the slander rejected in 68:2.
“We have made the Qur’an easy for remembrance”; the same divine plural joins ease to dhikr, showing how the “heavy word” can be accessible once given.
The repeated declaration that God made the Qur’an easy for remembrance reinforces that revelatory weight does not entail disabling hardship.
This third occurrence again couples divine facilitation with dhikr, a direct thematic meeting of the load removed and remembrance raised.
The fourth repeated assurance preserves the same ease-and-remembrance relation after successive warning narratives.
God says He made the Qur’an easy in the Prophet’s tongue so that people might remember; ease, the same addressee, speech, and remembrance meet explicitly.
God made the revelation easy in the Prophet’s tongue for glad tidings and warning; it specifies communicative ease in the mission whose strain the section recalls.

In the same surah that promises a heavy word, God knows the community cannot sustain the full night measure, turns toward them, and repeatedly commands recitation of what is easy; weight is retained while practice is lightened.
After the earth discharges its burdens and people are shown their deeds, whoever does an atom’s weight of good sees it; this ayah identifies one moral content disclosed from the hidden weight.
Whoever does an atom’s weight of evil sees it; paired with 99:7, this makes moral weight exact and personal after the earth’s burdens emerge.
Those whose scales are heavy are successful; moral heaviness in a just balance is favorable, reversing the section’s harmful heaviness on a back.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves; this ayah completes 7:8’s reversal by showing that lightness can be ruinous when what is weighed is righteous worth rather than a carried burden.
Those whose scales are heavy prosper; the repeated judgment formula keeps beneficial moral weight distinct from an oppressive load.
Those whose scales are light lose themselves in Hell; the result confirms that relief from a bodily burden and deficiency in the balance are opposite kinds of lightness.
The one whose scales are heavy enters a pleasing life; here weight signals sufficient good, not the damaging pressure heard in the section’s back.
The one whose scales are light has the abyss as refuge; it supplies the adverse boundary showing that “light” is not invariably the Qur’anic image of salvation.

The ẓihār formula derives its force from calling a wife like one’s mother’s back, yet the ayah rejects that speech as false; the same back root has a legal-idiomatic use wholly different from a load-bearing back.

One who returns after ẓihār must free an enslaved person before marital contact; the back-derived formula of 58:2 is answered with release from bodily bondage, joining two of the section’s secondary details.

The best speech makes the skins of those who fear God shiver, then their skins and hearts soften to God’s remembrance; like the creaking back, meaning becomes perceptible through bodily response, but here dhikr ends in softness.
After 9:14’s healing of believers’ breasts, God removes the rage of their hearts; this ayah’s own contribution is the taking away of an inward weight.

People reach needs held in their breasts by means of livestock, and are carried on them and on ships; chest, need, and being borne meet in one ayah, reversing the section’s human bearer into a carried passenger.
